name: Treadwheel
note: Winch or pump drive with ten or more people. Power output is constant, not pulsed like a crank.

name: Horse gin
note: Horizontal drive shaft for well pumping or mill gearing. More efficient than treadwheel; steady loading suits horse gait.

name: Undershot water wheel
note: This already operates at scale wherever there is a river to turn it. The water pushes on the bucket; it is simple, portable, and tolerates muddy water and sand.

name: Overshot water wheel
note: This already exists wherever a flowing stream gives a significant drop, and it is capable of real scale: Rome's 16-wheel Barbegal complex is the standing example. Weight of the water does the work; it needs a significant drop but delivers more power per wheel.

name: Breastshot water wheel
note: Water hits the wheel at mid-height, between overshot and undershot. Smeaton measured efficiency systematically: breastshot wins by combining gravity and impulse when head is moderate. This is how empirical engineering began.

name: Poncelet water wheel
note: Buckets enter water tangentially with curved shape to eliminate impact shock. Efficiency gain of 10 percent; needs precision forging and fit.

name: Fourneyron turbine
note: Radial outflow turbine with guide vanes and buckets at exact angles. Efficiency 80+ percent; requires machining to hold form under pressure.

name: Francis inward flow turbine
note: Spiral guide vanes and curved buckets; flow reverses direction inside runner. High efficiency (85+ percent) across wide head range; sensitive to blade wear.

name: Pelton turbine
note: A jet of water hits a double-cup bucket at high speed, splitting the jet tangentially to the wheel. Ideal for very high heads with low flow. The bucket profile is critical; casting is easier than machining but requires controlled cooling to avoid cracks.

name: Kaplan propeller turbine
note: Adjustable blade pitch changes angle under load; blade linkage responds to flow and head. Unique advantage in variable river flow; servo control needed.

name: Penstock and flume
note: Pressure pipes need metal bands or thicker wood. Open flumes are simpler but freeze and leak. Pressure drop matters; smooth bores reduce loss.

name: Draft tube (diffuser)
note: Diffuser expands flow to low speed below wheel; recovers energy that would waste. Increases effective head by several meters. Essential for efficient high-speed turbines.

name: Governor for water wheel
note: Mechanical governors sense wheel speed and throttle water supply. Feedback loop keeps speed near constant despite load changes. Enables textile machinery synchronisation.

name: Tide mill
kb: Impoundment captured by gates at high tide, released through wheel
note: A mill at the estuary with gates that open on incoming tide, close on outgoing, releasing a head of water. Twice per 24 hours, not continuous, but free and predictable. Requires careful site and sluice design.

name: Post mill
kb: Windmill on single central post, rotates whole body to face wind
note: The entire mill building pivots on a post to face the wind. It is portable, fits anywhere, and gives you wind power without a tall fixed tower. The miller rotates it by hand or rope from a tail pole.

name: Tower mill
kb: Fixed brick or stone tower, cap rotates to face wind
note: A fixed tapered brick or stone tower with a rotating cap. Taller and heavier than a post mill, it catches stronger winds and is more stable. The rotary bearing is now high stress, needing good metalwork.

name: Windmill fantail
note: A small perpendicular fan on the tail of the cap automatically rotates the mill to face the wind. If the wind is too strong, the fan spins faster, which tilts a striker linkage that furls the sail. No miller attendance needed at night.

name: Patent sail
note: Sail pivots on frame edges; spring loading and wind pressure itself cause sails to close partially in gust. No manual adjustment needed; automatic safety.

name: Spring sail
note: Springs hold sails at optimal angle; wind pressure changes angle automatically. Smoother response than patent sails; less jittering of mill speed.

name: Wind pump
note: Crank-driven pump lifts water into elevated tank; gravity feeds downstream. Works in flat terrain where water wheels are useless.

name: Wind electric generator
note: High-speed dynamo (hundreds of rpm) needs gearbox from slow mill rotation. Intermittent generation; requires battery storage or backup engine. Wind variability is limiting.

name: Atmospheric engine (Newcomen)
kb: Steam under atmosphere above piston, vacuum below pulls down
note: Steam below piston condenses; atmospheric pressure pushes down. Slow cycle (4-12 strokes per minute) but safe and robust. Cylinder cooling wastes most fuel.

name: Separate condenser (Watt)
note: Cylinder no longer cools and reheats every stroke, saving three-quarters of fuel. Condenser must be vacuum-tight and handle condensate without air leaks.

name: Double-acting cylinder
note: Piston rod must seal through cylinder end; rod packing leaks. Both ends push: halves cycle time and doubles power. Needs precise valve timing.

name: Parallel motion linkage (Watt)
note: Rhomboid frame keeps rod straight without cylinder guide; converts curved beam motion to linear. Enables long slender rods and compact designs.

name: Centrifugal governor (Watt)
note: Weights on spinning frame respond to centrifugal force; ball linkage adjusts throttle smoothly. Oscillates slightly around setpoint; feedback loop is inherently stable.

name: Sun and planet gear
note: Crank on planet cage allows working without infringing Newcomen patent. Gearing ratio is 1:1 but doubles rotations for same strokes. Smooth action.

name: High pressure steam engine
note: Much smaller and lighter than atmospheric engines for same power. But pressure vessel engineering is critical: failure mode is catastrophic explosion. Needs strong boiler...

name: Expansive working (cutoff)
note: Expanding steam does less work but fuel consumption falls more than power output. Efficiency gain of 20 percent. Requires precise valve timing and differential pressure sensing.

name: Cutoff valve (variable admission)
note: Simple slide valve with throttle edge; driver adjusts cutoff point manually or by governor. Critical surfaces must be flat and smooth to avoid leakage.

name: Corliss valve
note: Separate inlet and exhaust valves on cams; variable cutoff and independent release. Eliminates throttling losses. Needs high precision: each valve must seal dead stop.

name: Uniflow steam engine
note: Inlet at one end, exhaust ports in middle; piston always pushes exhaust out the same direction. Hot inlet end, cold exhaust end; eliminates cylinder temperature swing and...

name: Compound engine (two or three stage)
note: Expands steam over larger volume in stages; temperatures equalise between cylinders. Efficiency gain 50 percent over simple engine. Complex balance of pressures and speed...

name: Jet condenser
note: Simple direct condensation; very fast but air and water mix in condenser. Needs air pump to extract non-condensables. Uses more water than surface condenser.

name: Surface condenser
note: Water stays pure; no air mixing. Tubes must be straight and clean. Brass or copper tubes are expensive but necessary. Used in ships to allow boiler water recycling.

name: Feedwater heater
note: Reduces fuel needed to raise cold water to steam. Thermal efficiency gain 10-15 percent. Essential with high-pressure engines where feedwater is cold.

name: Economiser
note: Tubes in flue extract sensible heat that would otherwise waste up chimney. Fuel savings 15-20 percent. Works best with compound engines that run cooler than simple engines.

name: Haystack boiler
kb: Copper sphere or hemispherical shell, wood fire underneath
note: A rounded iron shell, fire at the bottom, the simplest boiler. Low pressure, small explosion risk, but slow steam generation and poor heat transfer. Used where durability matters more than speed.

name: Wagon boiler
kb: Cylindrical iron shell with flat ends, internal fire tube
note: Cylindrical shell, internal fire tubes passing through water. More surface area than haystack; faster steam generation. Mobile, used on early locomotives and threshing machines. Prone to scale and tube fouling.

name: Cornish boiler
kb: Cylindrical shell with two fire tubes inside
note: One large fire tube through the water. Rugged, handles high pressure, but prone to violent failure if the tube plugs and overheats. Requires skilled operation and routine inspection.

name: Lancashire boiler
kb: Cylindrical shell with two large internal fire tubes with return flues
note: Two fire tubes: more heat surface than Cornish, better steam generation. Smaller diameter tubes cool faster if they scale, less dramatic failure. Industrial standard for textile mills and pumping stations.

name: Locomotive boiler
note: Many tubes (hundreds) in compact space; high heating surface density. Flat crown sheet over firebox; supports massive pressure. Crown stays above water or it melts.

name: Water tube boiler
kb: Water flows through tubes between two large drums, fire outside
note: Small tubes of water through a chamber of hot gas, boiler in a steel frame. Much higher steam generation than fire-tube types, safer (small volume of water means less explosive stored energy), but more complex assembly and maintenance.

name: Babcock & Wilcox boiler
note: Straight tubes with headers at each end avoid expansion stresses. Tube ends are cup-expanded into header for seal. Very reliable and easy to repair.

name: Stirling boiler
note: Coil shape gives enormous surface area in compact space. Excellent heat transfer. Tendency to overheat the centre of the coil and thermal shock on water entry needs caref...

name: Safety valve (pop-off)
note: A weighted spring-loaded valve that lifts at a set pressure, and a Bourdon or liquid gauge to read it. Early boiler explosions killed many; this is the honest lesson that machines need observation and limits. Requires calibration and maintenance.

name: Pressure gauge
kb: Bourdon tube or diaphragm responds to pressure, needle shows reading
note: Curved tube straightens as pressure rises, moving needle. Scale must be calibrated. Essential for safe operation; missing gauge causes explosions from overpressure.

name: Steam trap
note: Thermostatic or float-based valve design; traps steam while draining water. Without traps, condensate backs up and blocks steam flow. Used on pipe runs and heat exchangers.

name: Superheater
kb: Tubes in flue gas heat saturated steam to 250+ C
note: Superheated steam (no moisture) expands more and reaches lower temperature at exhaust. Efficiency gain 10-15 percent. Tubes must resist corrosion; oxidation speeds up at ...

name: Impulse steam turbine (de Laval)
note: Single-stage design; steam expands in nozzle to high speed. All pressure drop occurs in nozzle. Very high rpm (up to 30,000). Needs reduction gear. Robust and simple.

name: Reaction steam turbine (Parsons)
note: Stages of rotor and stator blades; steam expands through each stage, doing work and accelerating. Above a few hundred kW, this beats reciprocating engines: no reciprocating masses, no vibration, compact, efficient. Blade tolerances and metallurgy are severe.

name: Curtis velocity-staged turbine
note: Nozzle, bucket row, intermediate nozzle, bucket row, etc. Compromise between simple de Laval and complex Parsons. Better efficiency than single-stage, simpler than reaction.

name: Turbine blade design and profile
note: Blade shape affects efficiency; small defects cause vibration and failure. Profile must be machined precisely; even 1 percent deviation costs 5 percent efficiency. Testin...

name: Turbine condenser and vacuum system
note: Vacuum pump (usually shaft-driven) pulls down to 0.05-0.1 atm. Every 0.1 atm reduction adds 5 percent efficiency. Air leaks from glands destroy vacuum; seals must be tight.

name: Reduction gear (turbine to load)
note: Turbines run 5000-30000 rpm; machinery needs 10-500 rpm. Single-stage helical gears give 10:1. Double-stage gives 100:1. Losses are 2 percent per mesh if teeth are cut precisely.

name: Coal gas engine (Otto silent gas engine)
note: Coal gas is sucked in, mixed with air, sparked, and exploded. Much lighter and simpler than a steam engine. No boiler, no furnace, no engineer. Otto and Diesel engines follow. Early models are unreliable; ignition is the problem.

name: Four-stroke cycle (Otto)
kb: Intake, compress, explode, exhaust strokes on one piston
note: Only one explosion per two revolutions; smooth operation with flywheel. Valve timing by cams is critical. Explosion pressure (50-100 psi) is much higher than steam engine...

name: Two-stroke cycle
note: Explosion every revolution; double power from same size. But exhaust scavenging is poor; unburnt fuel leaves and efficiency is lower. Simpler than four-stroke; no camshaft needed.

name: Compression ignition (Diesel cycle)
kb: Fuel injected during power stroke; self ignites from compression heat
note: Compression ratio 15:1 (vs 8:1 for petrol); explosion much more violent. Efficiency 40 percent (vs 25 percent Otto). Demands precision machining and strong materials.

name: Fuel injection system
note: Pump pressure 200+ atm; nozzles spray 10-100 micron droplets. Timing is critical (within 1 degree crank angle). Injector wear and coking cause poor spray. Precision manuf...

name: Hot bulb engine
note: Fuel drips into hot bulb; combustion is slow but sustained. Simple carburettor; no precision injection. Lower efficiency (25 percent) but robust and forgiving. Cheaper than Diesel.

name: Gas producer (wood or coal gasifier)
note: Fuel gas flows up through grate; water cooler removes tars. Engine burns mixed gas; lower calorific value than coal but simpler than retort and town gas system. No pipeline needed.

name: Carburetted engine
note: Spray nozzle meters fuel; Venturi air flow draws fuel into stream. Works because petrol evaporates readily. Float chamber maintains constant height. Much simpler than fue...

name: Poppet valve and camshaft
note: Cam profile controls valve opening duration and timing. Multiple cams on one shaft enable two or four valves per cylinder. Springs close valves; timing accuracy is critic...

name: Sleeve valve
note: Alternative to poppet valves; ports on sleeve line up with cylinder ports. Simpler timing but sleeve guides must have minimal clearance or it leaks. Machining cost high. ...

name: Supercharger (mechanically driven)
note: Rotor compressor (Roots blower style) compresses air continuously. Engine power increases 30-50 percent but heat and pressure rise. Intercooler needed to reduce inlet temperature.

name: Turbocharger (exhaust-driven)

name: Gas turbine (Brayton cycle)

name: Jet engine (turbojet)
note: Turbine exhaust gas expands through nozzle at high velocity for thrust. Fuel consumption enormous. Works only at high altitude where air is thin and speed is high. First ...

name: Rocket motor (solid or liquid fuel)
note: Solid grain burns with high velocity exhaust. Throat and nozzle diverter geometry critical. Liquid engines need pumps, injectors, and tanks. Combustion temperature 2000-3...

name: Liquid propellant systems
note: Pumps feed fuel and oxidiser to injector head. Stoichiometric ratio critical for combustion. Corrosion from reactive oxidisers; materials must resist liquid oxygen or aci...

name: Stirling hot air engine
note: Two cylinders with a hot end and cold end, connected via a regenerator. Displacement and timing are offset so heat is recycled. External combustion, any fuel, but complex mechanics and modest power. Useful for stationary engines where simplicity matters.

name: Compressed air engine
note: Air expands in cylinder; pressure drops as it does work. Efficiency only 40-50 percent because expansion is adiabatic. Storage vessel must be heavy; only practical for sm...

name: Hydraulic accumulator
note: Accumulates energy from steady pump; releases on demand. Piston or diaphragm separates water and air. Precharge air acts as spring. Used for peak load smoothing in factories.

name: Hydraulic power main (distribution network)
note: Pipe networks operated at 600-1000 psi; actuators lift, clamp, or oscillate. Simpler than belts and shafting. Quieter. Leakage and friction losses are higher than mechani...

name: Spring motor (large clockwork)
note: Energy storage for short duty; wind up before use. Power and duration trade off. Used in gramophones, mechanical toys. Not practical for sustained work.

name: Flywheel energy storage
kb: Heavy wheel spun up by engine stores kinetic energy
note: A massive disc or wheel, spun up and allowed to coast. Energy is stored as rotary momentum. Used in pumping stations to store water-mill power and release it on demand, or to smooth reciprocating engine output.

name: Dynamo (DC generator with self-excitation)
kb: Rotating coil in magnetic field, commutator rectifies alternating voltage to DC
note: Already in VOCABULARY as existing tech; referenced only.

name: Commutator (split ring rectifier)
note: Converts alternating coil voltage to pulsating DC at terminals. Brush contact is imperfect; arcing and wear occur. Performance depends on brush quality and speed (spark i...

name: Alternator (AC generator)
note: No commutator; coil output goes directly to terminals. Voltage and frequency both proportional to speed. Needs regulation for grid duty. Can supply transformers and polyp...

name: Exciter (small auxiliary generator)
note: Brushless excitation possible with rotating rectifier. Eliminates brush arcing. Field adjustable by rheostat; allows voltage regulation without mechanical governor.

name: Three-phase generation
note: Three phases carry power more uniformly than single phase. Mechanical power ripple decreases. Allows polyphase motors and delta/wye transformer configurations.

name: Transformer (step up and step down)
note: Two coils on an iron core; AC in one induces AC in the other at a different voltage. No moving parts, highly efficient. Allows voltage conversion without rotating machinery, the key to AC distribution.

name: Transmission line (high voltage power cable)
note: Transmission distance and voltage linked to loss; V^2 loss in fixed resistance. Long distances demand high voltage (10-100 kV). Copper cost dominates. Stranding allows flexibility.

name: Insulator (ceramic bushings)
note: Porcelain glaze prevents moisture absorption. Surface shape controls creepage path; longer path equals higher voltage withstand. Contamination and surface cracks cause failure.

name: Switchgear (high voltage switch)
note: Arcing at contact separation is intense; contacts must survive thousands of cycles. Oil-immersed switches cool the arc. Breaking capacity limited by arc voltage; cannot b...

name: Circuit breaker
note: Thermal or magnetic trip releases latched contacts. Oil bath quenches arc. Must be able to break fault current (thousands of amps). Manual reset after trip to prevent aut...

name: Fuse (wire or cartridge)
note: Simple one-shot protection; melts at exact current after precise time delay. Silver alloys reduce corrosion and resist vibration. Renewable fuses avoid replacement cost.

name: Lightning arrester (surge diverter)
note: Spark gap ionises at threshold voltage; conducts surge to earth. Must re-extinguish when surge passes to avoid continuous fault. Coordination of gap spacing is critical.

name: Substation (transformer station)
note: Receives high-voltage transmission lines, steps them down via transformers to local distribution voltage, distributes to neighborhoods and industries. A hub between generation and use; switching and protection equipment required.

name: Rotary converter (synchronous motor-generator)
note: Synchronous motor pulls polyphase AC, driving generator rotor that produces DC. Elegant but needs starting torque; rarely used. Motor-driven DC generator is simpler but l...

name: Lead acid storage battery
kb: Lead plates in sulfuric acid; charge with DC current
note: Lead oxide and lead plates in sulfuric acid: charge with DC, discharge to get power. Rechargeable, robust, stores significant energy. The acid eats organic matter and corrodes copper; wood cases and lead terminals are necessary.

name: Nickel-iron storage battery
note: Nickel oxide and iron electrodes in caustic soda solution. Tougher than lead-acid, tolerates abuse and overcharge, but lower voltage and self-discharge. Edson and Tesla championed it; it is still used in harsh environments.

name: Battery charging system
note: Regulates charge voltage to battery voltage plus drops. Overcharge kills battery and causes gassing. Undercharge reduces capacity. Thermal compensation for temperature dr...

name: Load factor and diversity management

name: Grid interconnection
note: Meshed networks improve reliability; single failures do not black out large areas. Voltage and frequency control complex. Fault analysis requires detailed model. Coordina...

name: Frequency standardisation (50 or 60 Hz)
note: Generators locked to mains frequency by synchronous motor action. Frequency drift causes oscillation between generators. Tight speed control with governors needed. Standa...

name: Power factor correction
note: Inductive loads lag voltage; capacitors lead and cancel reactive current. Reduces transmission line current for same real power, cutting I^2R losses. Improves voltage regulation.

name: Hydroelectric power station
kb: Multiple turbines in powerhouse with generators and transformers
note: A dam, penstock, turbine, and dynamo coupled: water flow becomes rotary motion becomes electrical current. The scale is decided by head and flow. Long-distance transmission at high voltage makes remote hydro economical.

name: Thermal power station (coal-fired)
note: Boiler efficiency 80 percent; turbine 40 percent; overall 32 percent. Condenser cooling is bottleneck; large volumes of water needed. Coal handling, ash disposal, and chi...

name: Pumped storage hydroelectric system
kb: Pump water uphill at night using cheap power; release through turbine at peak demand
note: Two reservoirs at different elevations: pump water up when power is cheap, run it down to generate when demand is high. Stores energy as gravitational potential; no battery needed. Requires two dams and good geology.

name: Charcoal production by burning
note: Yield 25 percent by weight; remainder is vapour and water. Charcoal burns hotter and leaves less ash than raw wood. Used as fuel and as reducing agent in metallurgy.

name: Coal mining and washing
note: Wet washery separates coal from rock by density. Gritty coal damages boiler tubes and mill machinery. Ash content 5-15 percent after washing; fuel value improves 20 percent.

name: Coke oven (beehive or by-product)
note: Coal volatiles driven off; coke (carbon and ash) remains. Beehive ovens discard gas. By-product ovens recover tar, ammonia, and gas for sale. Coke is cleaner fuel with le...

name: Town gas retort and generator

name: Gas holder (gasometer)

name: Oil drilling and production
note: Cable tool (impact) is simple but slow. Rotary rig (drilling mud) is faster for deep wells. Pump jack oscillates for shallow production. Well control difficult; blowouts ...

name: Oil refining and fractionation
note: Fractionating column with bubble trays or packing separates by boiling point. Gasoline, kerosene, fuel oil, and residue by temperature zones. Exact separation very diffic...

name: Oil cracking (thermal decomposition)
kb: Heavy oil fractions heated to break long-chain hydrocarbons
note: Heat cracks C20+ molecules into smaller molecules and olefins. Increases yield of gasoline and kerosene from heavy fractions. Furnace coking (carbon buildup) requires fre...

name: Kerosene (paraffin oil) production
note: Kerosene is a clear liquid fraction with a clean flame, brighter than candles or whale oil. Cheaper to refine than to ship coal. Lamps are simple: wick, chimney, brass fitting.

name: Petrol (gasoline) production
note: Ideal fuel for spark-ignited engines; high energy content and quick vaporisation. Octane rating (knock resistance) improves with aromatic content. Volatility must be cont...

name: Fuel oil (bunker oil) production
kb: 300-500 C boiling fraction from crude oil refining
note: Cheap and dense energy source for large stationary engines. Viscosity high; heating required for pumping in winter. Used in thermal power stations and ship propulsion after 1920.

name: Lubricating oil production
note: Viscosity and flash point selected for duty. High-speed machinery needs light oil (ISO 32); slow machinery needs heavy (ISO 100+). Paraffinic oils are cheapest; naphtheni...

name: Peat extraction and drying
note: Peat burns with much smoke and ash; energy content half of coal. Used in regions without coal (Ireland, Scandinavia). Moisture content critical; wet peat requires long drying.

name: Oil shale retorting
note: Retort temperature 500-600 C; oil vapours condense and collect. Residue char usable as fuel. Yield 10-15 percent by weight. Expensive compared to crude oil but valuable w...
